newsitem.title: TURKEY: Kurds to extend U.S. truce, keep Iraq out of feud.
newsitem.headline: Kurds to extend U.S. truce, keep Iraq out of feud.

text.p: Two rival Kurdish factions on Thursday agreed to extend a U.S.-brokered ceasefire that ended two months of clashes in northern Iraq and said they would not draw Iraq and Iran into their decades-old feud.

"All participants agreed...to maintain and strengthen the ceasefire with a view to making it permanent," U.S. peace envoy Robert Pelletreau said, reading a joint declaration after two days of talks in Ankara between the Kurdish groups.
Pelletreau brokered a ceasefire between the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) last week.
The clashes gave President Saddam Hussein a foothold in Western-protected northern Iraq after a five-year break and raised the spectre of Tehran coming into the conflict.
But Pelletreau said the Kurds had agreed not to call in Iranian or Iraqi help against each other.
"The parties agreed that they shall not seek the intervention of any other forces which could aggravate the conflict or raise tensions," he said.
The KDP of Massoud Barzani joined forces with Baghdad in late August to take the key city of Arbil from the PUK, prompting U.S. missile strikes against targets in southern Iraq.
Barzani accuses Iran of giving the PUK massive military aid. Both the PUK and Tehran deny this.
The Iraqi Kurds broke from Baghdad with Western encouragement after Iraq's defeat in the 1991 Gulf War but the fighting has rendered a power-sharing regional parliament obsolete.
A U.S.-led air force patrols an Iraqi no-fly zone over northern Iraq. The Iraqi official media assailed the United States for sponsoring the talks.
"The peace imposed by America (in northern Iraq)...is fragile and shaky because it is implemented in order to achieve American interests," the al-Iraq newspaper said.

Pelletreau, the assistant secretary of state for near eastern affairs, said the Kurds had also agreed "to reestablish peace and stability in northern Iraq by beginning a process of political reconcilitation" leading to elections in north Iraq.
Washington brought the factions to two rounds of peace talks in Ireland after fighting last year but no concrete settlement to their power struggle was reached.
They disagree over sharing the revenues from the KDP's makeshift oil trade on the Turkish border and control of Arbil, seat of the regional parliament.
A monitoring group, including members of the Turkoman and Assyrian minorities in northern Iraq, will ensure the ceasefire is adhered to, Pelletreau said.
The two groups are to hold further talks in Ankara on November 15.
